items.title: Father Al Lewis Interview, 1972-02-21
items.q: He taught me banjo... I was required to have a teacher to lead me on.

ctx.x: He taught me banjo. He taught me banjo, he taught Kimball's banjo, he taught Sales's banjo. But I was the last one that he taught. How old were you then? Well that's where I got the figure out. And Philip Boito, you know, got the music still down there. I took, when Willie Foster went back to St. Louis, he played up there. Well, we still worked for St. Louis, you know, the Boots used to leave town and go up there. Well, I got another teacher, he was at GC Coins, he was on Cronley Street then. Philip Boito, he…
What did Willie Foster teach you? How did he teach you the language?

items.title: Father Al Lewis Interview, 1972-02-21
items.q: And I got with Willie died. He died in Baton Rouge, about a year or so ago. And he left here. He lived in 8510 Corn Street. Well he had trouble with his wife, you know, like men do. You have trouble with some things like that. And he put me in an awkward position, because just at the time I thought

ctx.x: You didn't know your uncle's name that played music on there, that your mother played

the name? Where he's from? Oh well, my mother was born and growing up with Virginia. You understand? They came here from Virginia. She was a, what you call a practical nurse and they come down here. Well, it was a lady who used to live on 2nd Street, or Phillips City Street, I believe it was, Miss Cecilia Logan. She used to be the head training nurse at Hotel Duke. Well, she got my mother's job nursing, Chief O'Connor. Chief O'Connor was the chief of police at that time, you understand? And got her nursing around…
Who were playing with you then?

items.title: Father Al Lewis Interview, 1972-02-21
